notes: A calcium borate frit with one CaO to one B2O3 and no silica or alumina; Dutch recipes call it 'calciumboraatfritte 3221'. It is a concentrated boron source, chemically like colemanite without the water. Sold by Keramikos, Cock Keramiek, Ve-Ka and De Beeldhouwwinkel.
manufacturer: Sold under the Keramikos brand (Keramikos B.V., Haarlem, Netherlands); producer not stated
hazards: Leadless. Keramikos and Ve-Ka state that it is not classified as hazardous under CLP. Avoid breathing the dust.

source.name: Keramikos, product page 'Calciumboraat fritte 32.21 1 kg' (nominal composition)

name: Zinc Frit 32.22 (Keramikos)
notes: A zinc borosilicate frit with no alumina and about 29% ZnO. Dutch recipes use it to add zinc in fritted form, for matte, crystalline and zinc-dependent colour effects. Sold by Keramikos and Cock Keramiek.
manufacturer: Sold under the Keramikos brand (Keramikos B.V., Haarlem, Netherlands); producer not stated
hazards: Leadless. Keramikos and Cock Keramiek state that it is not classified as hazardous. Avoid breathing the dust.

source.name: Keramikos, product page 'zink fritte 32.22 1 kg' (Seger formula)

name: Alkali Frit 15.10 (Keramikos)
notes: A sodium-zinc alkali frit with no boron and little alumina: the classic Dutch 'alkalifritte 1510' for alkaline glazes such as turquoise copper blues, raku and crackle. Keramikos and Ve-Ka (as 'Alkali 2495') still sell it in 2026. Keramikos now also sells 'Alkali fritte 21.20' as its replacement.
manufacturer: Sold under the Keramikos brand (Keramikos B.V., Haarlem, Netherlands); producer not stated
hazards: Leadless. Keramikos states that it is not classified as hazardous under CLP. Avoid breathing the dust.

source.name: Keramikos, product page 'Alkali fritte 15.10 1 kg' (Seger formula)

name: Lead Bisilicate Frit 10.05 (Keramikos)
notes: Standard lead bisilicate frit (PbO·2SiO2 with a little alumina) for low-fired earthenware and majolica glazes; it is the Dutch counterpart of UK lead bisilicate. Sold by Cock Keramiek, Ve-Ka (as 3647) and De Beeldhouwwinkel (Keramikos 10.05).
manufacturer: Sold under the Keramikos brand and by other Dutch suppliers; producer not stated
hazards: CONTAINS LEAD (PbO about 65%). Cock Keramiek marks it 'Gevaarlijke stof'. Lead frits are classified in the EU as Repr. 1A and STOT RE 1. Reimbold & Strick's SDS for its lead frit A 1316 P lists: H302+H332 (harmful if swallowed or inhaled), H351 (suspected of causing cancer), H360Df (may damage the unborn child; suspected of damaging fertility), H372 (damages organs through prolonged exposure) and H410 (very toxic to aquatic life). Use it only with dust control, gloves and good hygiene, and keep it away from children and food areas. Lab-test any glaze made with it for lead release before it is used on food or drink surfaces.

source.name: Cock Keramiek, product page 'Fritte 10.05 Loodbisilicaat' (Seger formula)

name: Lead Monosilicate Frit (R&S A 1316 / M&M M 70)
notes: Lead monosilicate frit (one PbO to one SiO2), the most lead-rich standard frit. It is a very strong low-temperature flux for earthenware and raku glazes. Expansion is about 89-90 x 10^-7/K, with softening at about 450-470 °C. Sold to potters by Ve-Ka (Netherlands, as 2994). Ing. Lehrer (Austria) publishes the 2019 SDS for R&S A 1316 P.
manufacturer: Reimbold & Strick (Köln) as A 1316 and Mondré & Manz (Troisdorf) as M 70; the producer of the Dutch retail product is not stated
hazards: CONTAINS LEAD (PbO about 79%). Reimbold & Strick's SDS for A 1316 P (rev. 1.07, 2019) classifies it as Repr. 1A and STOT RE 1: H302+H332 (harmful if swallowed or inhaled), H351 (suspected of causing cancer), H360Df (may damage the unborn child; suspected of damaging fertility), H372 (damages organs through prolonged exposure) and H410 (very toxic to aquatic life). Use it only with dust control, gloves and good hygiene. Lab-test any glaze made with it for lead release before it is used on food or drink surfaces.

name: Eckalite 1 Kaolin
notes: Water-washed primary kaolin from Pittong near Ballarat, Australia's only hydrous kaolin plant; the standard Australian china clay for glazes and white bodies. Sold by Walker Ceramics (BA330), Pottery Supplies Online, The Potter's Market and others.
manufacturer: Green360 Technologies (formerly Suvo Minerals Australia; earlier Imerys Minerals Australia / ECC), Pittong, Victoria, Australia
hazards: SDS (Suvo Minerals Australia, Eckalite 1 & 1 Plus, 2024): kaolin >98%, crystalline silica (quartz) <1%. Avoid breathing the dust.

name: Eckalite 2 Kaolin
notes: A second Pittong kaolin grade, slightly more iron-bearing than Eckalite 1; sold to potters by Walker Ceramics (BA331, which replaced their Eckaglas), Northcote Pottery Supplies and Blackwattle Pottery. Used for glaze alumina, suspension and slips. Walker's figures are the ones it gave in 2007 for Eckaglas, the grade this replaced.
manufacturer: Green360 Technologies (formerly Suvo Minerals Australia; earlier Imerys Minerals Australia / ECC), Pittong, Victoria, Australia
hazards: Kaolin; the related Eckalite 1 SDS (2024) gives quartz <1%. Avoid breathing the dust.

name: New Zealand Halloysite (Imerys, Matauri Bay)
notes: Very white, low-iron, low-titania halloysite (a kaolin-group clay) separated from altered rhyolite at Matauri Bay; used for translucent porcelain and very clear glazes. Sold in Australia by Walker Ceramics (BA139) and in the US as 'Kaolin New Zealand'.
manufacturer: Imerys (New Zealand China Clays), Matauri Bay, Northland, New Zealand
hazards: Kaolin-group clay with fine tubular particles; the parent rock is quartz and cristobalite and traces may remain (the brochure's XRD shows both). Avoid breathing the dust.

name: Ball Clay CA1 / CA2 (Claypro, Axedale)
notes: Dry-milled, very plastic secondary clay from Claypro's own pit at Axedale, Victoria; the Australian ball clay sold to potters as CA1 (Northcote) and CA2 (Walker, Blackwattle). Used for plasticity in bodies and for suspension, silica and alumina in glazes.
manufacturer: Claypro Aust Pty Ltd, Junortoun (Bendigo); mined at Axedale, Victoria, Australia
hazards: Claypro SDS (2015): about 20% crystalline silica (quartz); classified Carcinogen Category 1A (H350, by inhalation). Avoid breathing the dust.

name: Clay Ceram (Unimin, Granville)
notes: A plastic, white-firing kaolinitic clay with ball-clay working properties, made to replace the older Cresta BB and BB4; it appears in older Australian recipes as 'Clay Ceram'. Walker Ceramics marks it 'no longer available'.

notes: A Thai potash feldspar of the kind now sold as 'potash feldspar' in Australia; Walker Ceramics lists its BA350 as Thai and Blackwattle's SDS names 'Potash Feldspar K200BL' (Scott Chemicals). name: Soda Feldspar (Walker BA340, India)
notes: Albite-type soda feldspar imported from India and sold by Walker Ceramics and Blackwattle Pottery; a glossier, slightly lower-melting flux than potash feldspar for stoneware and mid-fire glazes. Walker's figures date from 2007 and give no calcium, which Indian soda feldspars usually have.

name: Cornish Stone, Synthetic (Walker BA280)
notes: Walker's fluorine-free blend of minerals made to match natural Cornish stone; Walker describes it as a slightly weaker flux than feldspar, for recipes that call for Cornish stone. notes: Milled quartz flour (about 90% finer than 45 microns) from Sibelco's Lang Lang operation; the 'Silica 200#' sold by Walker (BA770), Keane, Northcote and Blackwattle. Walker's SDS names the Sibelco WQ series.
manufacturer: Sibelco Australia (formerly Unimin Australia), Lang Lang, Victoria, Australia

name: Ferro Frit 4110
notes: Lead-free, high-soda, high-expansion frit with a little boron. It was Ferro Australia's counterpart of US Frit 3110 and is named in many Australian recipes for copper turquoise, manganese purple and crackle glazes (Walker gives 980-1080°C, expansion 96 x10^-7). Walker Ceramics now supplies imported US Ferro 3110 in its place, and some shops still sell under the 4110 name, so check which frit you have.
Walker Ceramics listed it until February 2020, but no longer by March 2021.
manufacturer: Ferro Corporation (Aust.) Pty Ltd, now Vibrantz Technologies (Victoria, Australia)
hazards: No SDS seen. Frit is a ground glass with no free crystalline silica; avoid breathing the fine dust.

source.name: Wellington Potters Supplies (NZ), Frit compositions table

name: Ferro Frit 4124
notes: Lead-free calcium borosilicate frit, Ferro Australia's version of US Frit 3124 but with less alumina. It is a common base for earthenware glazes, including clear glazes over underglaze, at 1040-1100°C (Walker; expansion 74 x10^-7). Australian and NZ suppliers now sell US Ferro 3124 as its replacement; 3124 has more alumina, so a recipe written for 4124 may need a little less kaolin.
manufacturer: Ferro Corporation (Aust.) Pty Ltd, now Vibrantz Technologies (Victoria, Australia)
hazards: No SDS seen. Frit is a ground glass with no free crystalline silica; avoid breathing the fine dust.

source.name: Wellington Potters Supplies (NZ), Frit compositions table

name: Ferro Frit 4108
notes: Soft, lead-free, high-calcium borosilicate frit. It was Ferro Australia's counterpart of US Frit 3134, with a little alumina, and it appears in many older Australian earthenware and mid-fire recipes. Suppliers now sell US Ferro 3134 in its place, and Walker suggests 60% 3134-2 with 40% 3124 to imitate 4108.
Walker Ceramics already listed it as no longer available in October 2016.
manufacturer: Ferro Corporation (Aust.) Pty Ltd (Victoria, Australia)
hazards: No SDS seen. Frit is a ground glass with no free crystalline silica; avoid breathing the fine dust.

name: Ferro Frit 4064 (lead bisilicate)
notes: Standard low-solubility lead bisilicate frit (about 65% lead oxide) for bright, glossy earthenware glazes at 950-1050°C (Walker; expansion 72 x10^-7). It is sold in Australia as 4064 or 3531 by Walker Ceramics, Keane Ceramics, NR Pottery Supplies, Ipswich Pottery Supplies and Blackwattle Pottery ('Frit 3531 (replaces 4064)').
manufacturer: Ferro / Vibrantz Technologies (sold in Australia; current place of manufacture not stated)
hazards: LEAD FRIT: about 65% lead oxide, held in glass. Lead compounds are toxic if swallowed or inhaled, can harm fertility and the unborn child, and damage organs with repeated exposure. Avoid all dust, wear a P2/P3 respirator, wash after use, and keep it away from food areas and children. Glazes made with it must be correctly formulated and fired, and lead release from functional ware should be tested by a laboratory.

notes: Dense, lead-free, zircon-opacified white frit (about 12% ZrO2) for white and pastel earthenware glazes at 1040-1100°C (Walker; expansion 59 x10^-7). Walker Ceramics has sold Frit 9113 in its place since 2022 (listed for a time as 9117), but no analysis of 9113 is published.
manufacturer: Ferro Corporation (Aust.) Pty Ltd (Victoria, Australia)

name: Vibrantz Frit 90255
notes: A leadless, very low-expansion calcium-barium borosilicate frit (expansion 40 x 10^-7/K), high in silica and boron. Frits this low in expansion are added in small amounts to lower a glaze's expansion and cure crazing. On its own it is stiff (softening 910 °C, half-sphere point 1280 °C). Sold by Hans Wolbring (Höhr-Grenzhausen, Germany).
manufacturer: Vibrantz GmbH, Frankfurt am Main, Germany (formerly Ferro GmbH; the 90xxx numbers date from Degussa)
hazards: Leadless frit (glass, CAS 65997-18-4) with about 6% barium oxide and 22% boron oxide bound in the glass. No SDS was found for this product. Some EU suppliers label boron-rich frits as toxic to reproduction (H360FD), so check the SDS that comes with the bag. Avoid breathing the dust.

name: Vibrantz Frit 90428
notes: A leadless calcium-zinc borosilicate frit with a little lithium and barium, sold for matte to satin-matte effect glazes. Expansion is 70 x 10^-7/K; transformation 555 °C, softening 740 °C, half-sphere point 970 °C. Sold by BSZ Keramikbedarf (which names Vibrantz GmbH, Frankfurt, as maker) and Hans Wolbring.
manufacturer: Vibrantz GmbH, Frankfurt am Main, Germany (formerly Ferro GmbH; the 90xxx numbers date from Degussa)
hazards: Leadless frit (glass, CAS 65997-18-4) with about 6% barium oxide and 7% zinc oxide bound in the glass. No SDS was found for this product. Barium in a frit is much less soluble than barium carbonate, but test any barium glaze for leaching before it is used on food surfaces. Avoid breathing the dust.
